groups.label: Look Back
items: Five years after the Revolution: The French Revolution begins in 1789 with the Storming of the Bastille. The slogan Liberté, égalité, fraternité was proclaimed — and five years later, in 1794, the National Convention extended it to enslaved populations in French territories.

Haitian Revolution trigger: The major slave revolt in Saint-Domingue began in 1791. It took 3 years of intense fighting on the island before Paris formally ratified full emancipation in 1794. The sequence: 1789 → 1791 → 1794.

groups.label: Year of 1794
items: 1794 is the height of the Reign of Terror — Robespierre is executed that same July. The National Convention was in its most radical phase, the same political energy that pushed through abolition.

Toussaint Louverture, the future leader of Haiti, was already a rising military commander in Saint-Domingue by 1794 — the same year France's decree legally caught up to the revolution already underway on the ground.

groups.label: Look Ahead
items: Napoleon reverses the decree in 1802 — just eight years later. A short-lived window of legal freedom under French law: 1794 to 1802.
Haiti declares full independence in 1804, ten years after France's abolition decree — a straight line from legal emancipation to the colony's break from France.

France was the first major European colonial power to abolish slavery in 1794. Britain followed: subtract 13 years to reach the abolition of the British slave trade in 1807, or 40 years to reach Britain's full abolition of slavery in 1834.

groups.label: Look Back
items: Count forward from Hertz: Heinrich Hertz proved electromagnetic waves exist in 1887–88. Marconi turns that pure theory into a practical device about 7-8 years later, in 1895.
Sequential Tech Link: Hertz (1887) → Marconi (1895). Eight years from 'waves exist' to 'send a message with them.'

groups.label: Year of 1895
items: 1895 was the birth year of two mass-communication technologies: wireless radio (Marconi) and cinema (Lumière brothers). Both born the same year.
The '1-8-9-5' bridge trick: Röntgen also discovered X-rays in 1895. Pair 'invisible waves' (X-rays) with 'invisible signals' (radio) — both in 1895.

groups.label: Look Ahead
items: Turn of the Century Anchor: 1895 = exactly 5 years before 1900. A late-Victorian invention, not a 1930s one.
Marconi → Atlantic → 1901: 1895 = local demo. Six years later, 1901 = transatlantic signal.
Titanic anchor: Wireless saved survivors in 1912. Subtract ~17 years → 1895, when the technology was first demonstrated.

groups.label: Look Back
items: Northern Kingdom anchor: The Kingdom of Israel (the North) fell to the Assyrians in 722 BCE. Judah (the South) survived for another 134 years before Jerusalem fell to Nebuchadnezzar II in 588–586 BCE.
Nebuchadnezzar II becomes king of Babylon in 605 BCE, the same year he crushes Egypt at Carchemish. Jerusalem's conquest follows about 17 years into his reign, in 588 BCE.

Count forward from the first deportation: Babylon exiles King Jehoiachin and part of Jerusalem's elite in 597 BCE. The final conquest and the Temple's destruction come about nine years later, in 588 BCE.

groups.label: Year of 588 BCE
items: 588 BCE comes just one generation after Babylon itself broke free of Assyrian rule in 626 BCE — the new Babylonian Empire wasted little time turning to conquer its neighbors.
Greek philosopher Thales of Miletus predicts a solar eclipse around 585 BCE, just three years after Jerusalem's fall — a useful cross-check if you know early Greek science dates.

groups.label: Look Ahead
items: Cyrus the Great conquers Babylon in 539 BCE, ending the exile. Subtract 49 years from that to land on 588 BCE, when the exile began.
Second Temple bookend: Solomon's First Temple was destroyed by Babylon in 588/586 BCE. The Second Temple was destroyed by the Romans in 70 CE — over 650 years later.

groups.label: Look Back
items: Count forward from the English Civil War: fighting between King Charles I and Parliament breaks out in 1642. Seven years of war and political maneuvering later, the king is tried and executed in 1649. Think: seven years from civil war to regicide.
The Mayflower sails for the New World in 1620. Charles I is executed 29 years later, in 1649 — roughly one generation after the Pilgrims left England.

groups.label: Year of 1649
items: 1649 falls almost exactly at the midpoint of the 17th century — a king beheaded just one year shy of the century's halfway mark.
England abolishes the monarchy and declares itself a Commonwealth in the same year, 1649 — the execution and the birth of the republic happen together.

groups.label: Look Ahead
items: Restoration anchor: Charles I was executed in 1649, and the monarchy returned just 11 years later in 1660 when Charles II was restored to the throne. Think: 'Charles dies → 11 years → Charles returns.'
The Glorious Revolution came 39 years after Charles I's execution, in 1688. The long struggle over the power of Crown and Parliament continued from 1649 toward the constitutional settlement of 1688.

French Revolution comparison: The execution of Charles I in 1649 predates the execution of Louis XVI of France in 1793 by 144 years — England set the precedent for regicide long before France followed.

groups.label: Event Timeline
items: 1642 — Charles I raises his standard at Nottingham; the English Civil War begins
1645 — New Model Army formed; decisive Parliamentarian victory at the Battle of Naseby breaks Royalist power
1646 — Charles surrenders to the Scottish army, who hand him to Parliament the following year
1648 — Second Civil War; Pride's Purge removes moderate MPs, leaving the 'Rump Parliament' that will try the king
Jan 30, 1649 — Charles I tried, convicted of treason, and beheaded outside the Banqueting House in London

groups.label: Look Back
items: Magna Carta anchor: Magna Carta was sealed in 1215. Bannockburn came 99 years later, in 1314 — almost exactly a century from Magna Carta to Scotland's great victory over England.
William Wallace wins the Battle of Stirling Bridge in 1297, near the same ground. Bannockburn comes 17 years later, in 1314, finishing what Wallace started.
Edward I, the 'Hammer of the Scots,' dies in 1307. Just seven years after his death, his son Edward II suffers the humiliating defeat at Bannockburn in 1314.

groups.label: Year of 1314
items: The Knights Templar are dissolved and their last Grand Master burned at the stake in 1314 — the same year, on the other side of Europe, Robert the Bruce was securing Scotland's independence.
1314 sits early in the fourteenth century, a full generation before the Black Death reaches Europe in 1347 — a useful anchor if you know the plague date.

groups.label: Look Ahead
items: Declaration of Arbroath anchor: Scotland sent the famous Declaration of Arbroath to the Pope asserting independence in 1320 — just 6 years after the military triumph at Bannockburn in 1314.
Treaty of Edinburgh-Northampton anchor: England formally recognized Scottish independence in 1328, 14 years after Bannockburn. Subtract 14 from 1328 to land on 1314.
The Hundred Years' War between England and France breaks out in 1337, just 23 years after Bannockburn — England was still nursing its Scottish defeat when it turned to fight France next.

groups.label: Look Back
items: The Bay of Pigs invasion fails in 1961 — a botched US attempt to overthrow Castro. Just one year later, in 1962, Soviet missiles show up in Cuba, a direct consequence of Castro turning to Moscow for protection after the invasion.
The Berlin Wall goes up in August 1961. About a year later, in October 1962, Cold War tension peaks again with missiles in Cuba — two back-to-back Cold War flashpoints.

groups.label: Year of 1962
items: John Glenn becomes the first American to orbit Earth in February 1962, the same year the Cuban Missile Crisis unfolds in October — space-race triumph and nuclear near-disaster in the same year.
The crisis lasted thirteen days in October 1962. The number 13 helps lock in the year: thirteen tense days in '62.

groups.label: Look Ahead
items: Kennedy was assassinated in November 1963, just over a year after the crisis. Think: 1962 = missiles; 1963 = Dallas.
The Nuclear Test Ban Treaty is signed in 1963, one year after the crisis — a direct result of both superpowers stepping back from the brink they reached in 1962.

groups.label: Event Timeline
items: Oct 16, 1962 — Kennedy briefed on U-2 spy photos showing Soviet missile sites under construction in Cuba
Oct 22, 1962 — Kennedy's televised address reveals the crisis; US naval blockade of Cuba begins
Oct 24, 1962 — Soviet cargo ships approach the blockade line, then stop and turn back
Oct 27, 1962 — 'Black Saturday': a U-2 is shot down over Cuba; another strays into Soviet airspace; war feels imminent
Oct 28, 1962 — Khrushchev announces Soviet missiles will be withdrawn; crisis ends

groups.label: Look Back
items: World War II ends in 1945. Just three years later, in 1948, Israel is established — the Holocaust's aftermath directly accelerated international support for a Jewish state.

The Balfour Declaration, Britain's pledge of support for a Jewish homeland in Palestine, comes in 1917. Israel's founding follows 31 years later, in 1948 — roughly a generation from promise to statehood.

groups.label: Year of 1948
items: Mahatma Gandhi is assassinated in India in January 1948, and Israel declares independence in May 1948. Pair 'Gandhi dies' with 'Israel founded' to make the year 1948 stick.
The Universal Declaration of Human Rights is adopted by the UN in December 1948, the same year Israel is established — two major postwar milestones in international order, months apart.

groups.label: Look Ahead
items: Suez Crisis bridge: Israel's founding in 1948 was followed by its next major conflict, the Suez Crisis, 8 years later in 1956.
Six-Day War anchor: The Six-Day War happens in 1967, 19 years after Israel's founding. Subtract 19 from 1967 to land on 1948.
Camp David Accords anchor: Israel and Egypt sign the Camp David Accords in 1978, 30 years after Israel's establishment — three decades from founding to its first peace treaty with an Arab neighbor.

groups.label: Look Back
items: The Spanish Armada is defeated in 1588, one of Elizabeth's greatest triumphs. Fifteen years later, in 1603, she dies, having outlived her most famous victory by over a decade.
Elizabeth I becomes queen in 1558. She dies 45 years later, in 1603, after one of the longest reigns in English history up to that point.

groups.label: Year of 1603
items: 1603 marks a major royal transition: Elizabeth I dies and James VI of Scotland becomes James I of England, beginning the Stuart dynasty. Think 'Elizabeth ends → James begins' in 1603.
1603 sits between two famous landmarks: Elizabeth I dies in 1603, and the Gunpowder Plot to blow up Parliament is uncovered just two years later, in 1605.

groups.label: Look Ahead
items: The Gunpowder Plot is uncovered in 1605, just two years after Elizabeth's death. Think 1603 → Elizabeth dies; 1605 → Guy Fawkes and the failed plot to blow up Parliament.
The English Civil War begins in 1642, 39 years after Elizabeth's death. The Tudor age ended in 1603; within four decades, England would be fighting a civil war and eventually executing a king.

groups.label: Look Back
items: The first Olympic Games are traditionally dated to 776 BCE, just 23 years before Rome's legendary founding in 753 BCE — two foundational myths of the ancient Mediterranean world, born within a generation of each other.
Roman writers linked their city's origins back to the fall of Troy, traditionally placed around 1184 BCE — over 400 years before Rome's own legendary founding date.

groups.label: Year of 753 BCE
items: A useful number trick: 'seven-five-three' — Rome's traditional story begins in 753 BCE.

753 BCE is a purely legendary date, calculated centuries later by the Roman scholar Varro — less a historical fact than a founding myth, similar to how other ancient cultures gave their cities a symbolic origin story.

groups.label: Look Ahead
items: The Roman Republic traditionally began in 509 BCE, 244 years after the founding of Rome. Think 753 BCE → kings; 509 BCE → Republic.
Julius Caesar was assassinated in 44 BCE. From Rome's traditional founding in 753 BCE to Caesar's death is just over 700 years — a useful reminder of how long the Roman story lasted.

groups.label: Look Back
items: Spain becomes a republic in 1931, five years before civil war breaks out in 1936, as tensions between left and right factions build toward open conflict.
Hitler comes to power in Germany in 1933. Three years later, in 1936, the Spanish Civil War begins, with Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy supporting Franco's Nationalists.

groups.label: Year of 1936
items: 1936 is also the year Hitler hosts the Berlin Olympics and remilitarizes the Rhineland — the same year fascist and authoritarian forces are testing their strength across Europe, Spain included.
The Spanish Civil War begins in 1936, just three years before World War II erupts in 1939. It is often called a dress rehearsal for the larger war soon to follow.

groups.label: Look Ahead
items: World War II begins in 1939, three years after the Spanish Civil War starts. Subtract 3 from 1939 to land on 1936.
Franco rules Spain as dictator until his death in 1975, 39 years after the war began in 1936 — the conflict's winner held power for nearly four decades afterward.

groups.label: Look Back
items: Edwin Drake begins drilling near Titusville, Pennsylvania in 1858, using a steam engine borrowed from salt-well drilling techniques. He strikes oil the following year, in 1859.
Darwin anchor: Charles Darwin published On the Origin of Species in 1859. Pair 'oil underground' with 'evolution' — two revolutionary developments in the same year.

groups.label: Year of 1859
items: 1859 is also the year Charles Darwin publishes On the Origin of Species — the same year one discovery reshaped biology while another, quietly in Pennsylvania, was about to reshape energy and industry.
1859 sits right before the outbreak of the American Civil War in 1861 — Drake's well strikes oil just two years before the war that would soon demand more fuel and industry than ever.

groups.label: Look Ahead
items: John D. Rockefeller founds Standard Oil in 1870, eleven years after Drake's well. Subtract 11 from 1870 to land on 1859.
Karl Benz patents the first commercial gasoline automobile in 1886 — add 27 years to Drake's 1859 discovery to reach the moment oil found its defining new purpose.

groups.label: Look Back
items: India's Chandrayaan-2 attempted a lunar landing in 2019 but its lander crashed during the final descent. Four years later, Chandrayaan-3 achieved the landing in 2023.
The first human Moon landing was Apollo 11 in 1969. Chandrayaan-3 came 54 years later, in 2023 — more than half a century after humans first walked on the Moon.

groups.label: Year of 2023
items: 2023 is also the year Russia's Luna-25 mission crashed attempting the same south-pole landing, just days before Chandrayaan-3 succeeded — a striking same-year contrast between failure and success.
ChatGPT's public release caused a massive AI boom starting in late 2022 and through 2023 — the same year India made its own historic technological leap, on the Moon rather than in software.

groups.label: Look Ahead
items: China lands its Chang'e-6 mission on the Moon's far side in 2024, one year after Chandrayaan-3 — back-to-back lunar milestones from Asian space programs.
India plans a crewed Moon landing by 2040. Chandrayaan-3 in 2023 marks the first major stepping stone toward that goal — 17 years before the target.

groups.label: Look Back
items: The Seven Years' War ends in 1763, reshaping global trade and colonial economics. Thirteen years later, in 1776, Smith publishes his landmark critique of mercantilism.
The American Revolution began in 1775. One year later, in 1776, Adam Smith published The Wealth of Nations on the very same day the colonies declared independence.

groups.label: Year of 1776
items: 1776 is one of the most memorable years in history: the American Declaration of Independence and The Wealth of Nations were both published the same year. Pair 'political freedom' with 'economic freedom' — both in 1776.
Think 1776 = Jefferson and Adam Smith. The colonies were challenging political authority while Smith was questioning how economies should be organised.

groups.label: Look Ahead
items: The French Revolution begins in 1789, 13 years after Smith's book, partly fueled by the economic grievances he analyzed. Subtract 13 from 1789 to land on 1776.
Smith dies in 1790, just fourteen years after publishing his masterwork — long enough to see it become the foundational text of classical economics.

groups.label: Look Back
items: Alexander Fleming started working on bacteriology and antiseptics during World War I. About a decade after the war ends in 1918, his famous accidental discovery in the lab follows from that background — landing in 1928.
Charles Lindbergh made the first solo nonstop transatlantic flight in 1927. One year later, in 1928, Fleming discovered penicillin.

groups.label: Year of 1928
items: 1928 is also the year Amelia Earhart becomes the first woman to fly across the Atlantic — two very different breakthroughs, one in the sky and one in a petri dish, the same year.
1928 is the year of the first Academy Awards ceremony and the signing of the Kellogg-Briand Pact — think '1928 = penicillin and the beginning of the Hollywood awards era.'

groups.label: Look Ahead
items: The stock market crashes in 1929, just one year after Fleming discovered penicillin. Think 1928 → penicillin; 1929 → Wall Street crashes.
Penicillin isn't mass-produced until World War II, around 1943 — 15 years after its discovery. Subtract 15 from 1943 to land on 1928.
Fleming shares the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1945, 17 years after his original discovery — it took nearly two decades for the finding to be fully recognized and put to wide use.

groups.label: Event Timeline
items: 1928 — Fleming notices a mold (Penicillium notatum) has killed bacteria on a culture plate left near an open window
1929 — Fleming publishes his findings; few scientists take notice, and he cannot isolate the active compound
1939–40 — Howard Florey and Ernst Chain at Oxford purify penicillin and run the first animal tests
1942 — First human patient successfully treated; US and UK governments fund mass production for the war effort
1945 — Fleming, Florey, and Chain share the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine

groups.label: Look Back
items: Philip II of Macedon is assassinated in 336 BCE, two years before Alexander crosses into Asia in 334 BCE — the young king moves fast, securing Greece and launching his invasion within two years of taking the throne.

The Persian Wars, when Greece repelled Persian invasions at Marathon (490 BCE) and Salamis (480 BCE), end more than 140 years before Alexander goes on the offensive in 334 BCE — he's finally turning the tables on the old invader.

groups.label: Year of 334 BCE
items: 334 BCE falls in the same century as Aristotle's peak teaching years — Aristotle personally tutored Alexander as a boy, and just a few years later his student is crossing into Asia to conquer an empire.
334 BCE sits almost exactly 290 years before Julius Caesar's assassination in 44 BCE — a useful bridge if you know Caesar's date well.

groups.label: Look Ahead
items: Alexander dies in 323 BCE, just 11 years after beginning his conquests in 334 BCE — one of history's shortest windows between a campaign's start and an empire's peak.
The decisive Battle of Gaugamela, which breaks Persian resistance for good, happens in 331 BCE, three years after the campaign begins. Subtract 3 from 331 to land on 334 BCE.

groups.label: Event Timeline
items: 336 BCE — Philip II of Macedon is assassinated; Alexander, aged 20, inherits the throne
334 BCE — Alexander crosses the Hellespont into Asia Minor and wins his first major battle against the Persians at the Granicus River
333 BCE — Alexander defeats Darius III at the Battle of Issus, forcing the Persian king to flee
332 BCE — Alexander conquers Egypt without resistance and founds the city of Alexandria
331 BCE — Decisive victory over Darius III at Gaugamela effectively ends the Persian Empire's resistance

groups.label: Look Back
items: Charles II is restored to the throne in 1660, 28 years before the Glorious Revolution in 1688 — the Stuart monarchy that had been briefly abolished under Cromwell gets deposed again, this time for good, less than three decades later.
James II becomes king in 1685, just three years before Parliament invites William of Orange to invade in 1688 — a remarkably short reign before his own subjects push him out.

groups.label: Year of 1688
items: 1688 sits almost exactly a century before the French Revolution begins in 1789 — England settles its power struggle between Crown and Parliament peacefully, roughly 100 years before France does it violently.
1688 falls 39 years after the execution of Charles I in 1649 — father beheaded by Parliament, son restored and later deposed by it, all within one Stuart family saga.

groups.label: Look Ahead
items: The English Bill of Rights is passed in 1689, one year after William and Mary take the throne. Subtract 1 from 1689 to land on 1688.

The Act of Union merges England and Scotland into Great Britain in 1707, 19 years after the Glorious Revolution — the new constitutional settlement of 1688 held firm long enough to absorb an even bigger political change two decades later.

groups.label: Event Timeline
items: 1685 — James II, a Catholic, becomes king, alarming a largely Protestant Parliament
June 1688 — James II's son is born, raising fears of a Catholic dynasty; Parliament invites William of Orange to intervene
Nov 1688 — William lands at Torbay with an invasion force; James II's support collapses almost immediately
Dec 1688 — James II flees to France without a major battle being fought
Feb 1689 — William and Mary are jointly declared king and queen after accepting the Bill of Rights

groups.label: Look Back
items: Indian National Congress anchor: The INC is founded in 1885, giving Indian nationalism its first organized political voice. Twenty years later, in 1905, Curzon's partition transforms Congress from a moderate group into a mass nationalist movement.
Queen Victoria dies in 1901. Just four years into the new Edwardian era, in 1905, the Partition of Bengal ignites the Swadeshi movement — an early crack in British authority.

groups.label: Year of 1905
items: 1905 is also the year of the Russian Revolution of 1905, when workers and peasants rise against the Tsar — the same year colonial subjects in Bengal rise against British rule, half a world apart.
Einstein publishes his special theory of relativity in 1905, his 'miracle year.' The same year, a very different kind of upheaval — political rather than scientific — reshapes Bengal.

groups.label: Look Ahead
items: The All-India Muslim League is founded just one year later, in 1906 in Dhaka — the Partition of Bengal directly catalyzed the communal politics that would shape the subcontinent for decades.

The partition is reversed in 1911, six years later, under massive public pressure — a rare colonial reversal. The same year, the British shift their imperial capital from Calcutta to Delhi. Subtract 6 from 1911 to land on 1905.
Gandhi returns to India in 1915, ten years after the partition, and later builds directly on the Swadeshi boycott tactics pioneered in 1905 for his own independence campaigns.
